title: Cardiovascular Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium
path: Cardiovascular Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium

headings.title: Introduction to Maternal Cardiovascular Adaptations
headings.content: Pregnancy initiates a remarkable cascade of physiological adjustments designed to support the growing metabolic demands of the foetus while safeguarding maternal organs. The maternal cardiovascular system undergoes extensive remodeling starting as early as the fourth to sixth week of gestation. These changes prepare the body for the high volume demands of labour and the immediate blood loss that occurs during delivery. Hormonal influences, particularly progesterone and oestrogen, orchestrate systemic vasodilation and vascular compliance. Understanding these baseline alterations helps differentiate normal gestational physiology from pathological cardiovascular disease in clinical practice.

headings.title: Hemodynamic Changes and Blood Volume Expansion
headings.content:
Total blood volume increases significantly by approximately 40 to 50 percent above pre-pregnant levels, peaking around the thirty-fourth week of gestation. This expansion consists of a disproportionately greater rise in plasma volume compared to red blood cell mass, resulting in physiological anaemia of pregnancy due to hemodilution. 

- **Plasma Volume**: Increases by up to 50% to accommodate the low-resistance vascular bed of the placenta and protect the mother against postpartum hemorrhage.
- **Red Blood Cell Mass**: Increases by 20 to 30%, which is stimulated by elevated maternal erythropoietin production.
- **Hemodilution**: Drops average hemoglobin levels and hematocrit, though iron supplementation is routinely prescribed in Nigerian antenatal clinics to support this erythropoiesis.

headings.title: Cardiac Output and Structural Heart Modifications
headings.content: Cardiac output increases by 30 to 50 percent during pregnancy, driven primarily by an elevated stroke volume and a moderate rise in resting heart rate by about 10 to 15 beats per minute. Structural adaptations accompany these functional shifts. Because of the enlarging uterus elevating the diaphragm, the heart is displaced upward and to the left. Electrocardiograms may reveal a left axis deviation and transient Q-wave changes. On physical auscultation, a benign systolic ejection murmur and an exaggerated split first heart sound are common clinical findings that do not necessarily indicate underlying organic heart disease.

headings.title: Blood Pressure Variations and Systemic Vascular Resistance
headings.content: Systemic vascular resistance drops remarkably during pregnancy due to the relaxing effects of progesterone and local vasodilatory prostaglandins on vascular smooth muscle. Consequently, systemic blood pressure typically decreases during the first and second trimesters, reaching its nadir around mid-pregnancy before gradually returning toward pre-pregnant baseline values near term. Midwife assessments must account for this physiological dip so that true gestational hypertension is not masked, nor normal variations misdiagnosed as shock.

headings.title: Vena Cava Compression and Postural Hypotension
headings.content: In the third trimester, the gravid uterus can severely compress the inferior vena cava and descending aorta when the woman lies in the supine position. This compression obstructs venous return to the heart, sharply reducing preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output. This phenomenon, known as supine hypotensive syndrome, causes dizziness, pallor, cold sweat, and maternal hypotension. Midwives must consistently advocate for lateral positioning, particularly the left lateral tilt, to relieve vascular occlusion and maintain adequate uteroplacental perfusion.

headings.title: Cardiovascular Adjustments During Labour and Delivery
headings.content: Labour places intense hemodynamic stress on the maternal heart. With each uterine contraction, blood is autotransfused from the uteroplacental bed back into the systemic circulation, temporarily increasing cardiac output by an additional 15 to 25 percent in the first stage and up to 50 percent in the second stage. Pain, anxiety, and physical exertion further elevate heart rate and blood pressure. Adequate pain management and careful positioning during contractions are vital nursing interventions to prevent acute cardiac decompensation, especially in parturients with pre-existing cardiac disease.

headings.title: Cardiovascular Adjustments in the Puerperium
headings.content: Following delivery of the placenta, the removal of the low-resistance uteroplacental vascular bed triggers a massive autotransfusion of blood into the maternal circulation. Cardiac output transiently surges immediately postpartum before declining rapidly over the next two weeks. Diuresis occurs as extracellular fluid is mobilized and excreted, resolving pregnancy-induced hypervolemia. Most cardiovascular parameters return to non-pregnant baseline levels by six to twelve weeks postpartum, completing the physiological circle of gestation.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Nursing Assessment for Midwifery Practice
headings.content: Recognizing the fine line between normal pregnancy adaptation and cardiovascular pathology is a cornerstone of safe midwifery care. Midwives must perform thorough baseline assessments during antenatal booking and remain vigilant for red-flag symptoms such as severe dyspnoea, orthopnoea, chest pain, syncope, or persistent resting tachycardia. In high-resource and low-resource settings alike, identifying abnormal hemodynamic signs early prevents maternal morbidity and mortality associated with conditions like peripartum cardiomyopathy and pre-eclampsia.
